title: With the Childlike People

teacherSummary.text: Siddhartha works for Kamaswami but treats business as a game, caring little for profit, which irritates the merchant yet makes Siddhartha successful. He watches ordinary people—the 'childlike people'—with amusement as they suffer over money and desire. Kamala teaches him the art of love, and they agree that neither of them can truly love.

Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: “Expertise” here means: special skill or knowledge. In With the Childlike People, paragraph 36, Siddhartha tells Kamaswami that prices of fish and interest on loans are the merchant’s own fields of knowledge.

items.text: Reread: “But daily, at the hour appointed by her, he visited beautiful Kamala, wearing pretty clothes, fine shoes, and soon he brought her gifts as well.” What does “appointed” mean here, and what is literally happening in this line?
items.lookFor: appointed: fixed or set in advance.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: “Appointed” here means: fixed or set in advance. In With the Childlike People, paragraph 29, every day Siddhartha visits Kamala at the time she has chosen, now dressed well and bringing gifts.

items.text: What does “With the Childlike People” suggest about detachment among the childlike people? State the inference and the line that supports it.
items.lookFor: A stated inference (for example, that his detachment keeps him from being hurt but also from living) backed by one located line, such as the one in With the Childlike People, paragraph 37.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The chapter suggests that his detachment keeps him from being hurt but also from living. Support: “Indeed his soul was not with the trade.” (With the Childlike People, paragraph 37)

items.text: Find one example of characterization in this chapter. What does it reveal that a plain statement would not?
items.lookFor: Look for what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Kamaswami’s first appearance (“a swiftly, smoothly moving man with very gray hair, with very intelligent, cautious eyes” (With the Childlike People, paragraph 2)) shows a careful man ruled by worry, the opposite of Siddhartha’s calm.

items.text: How does the irony in this chapter shape what we understand about detachment among the childlike people?
items.lookFor: Look for gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The irony is that the man who despises the childlike people begins to want what they have: “wished that he would also be gifted with the ability to participate in all of this childlike-naive occupations of the day” (With the Childlike People, paragraph 39). His detachment is becoming a lack.

items.text: In the passage that begins “Siddhartha went to Kamaswami the merchant, he was directed into a rich house, servants led him between precious carpets into a chamber, where he awaited the master of the house.”, why might Hesse have chosen these particular words? Pick two and explain their connotations.
items.lookFor: Diction analysis of two words in the anchor passage.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: In With the Childlike People, paragraph 1, words of wealth (“rich house,” “precious” things) build the merchant’s world before the man appears; Siddhartha enters it as a guest, not a convert.

items.text: What causes the main turn in “With the Childlike People”, and what effect is it likely to have on what follows?
items.lookFor: Siddhartha works for Kamaswami but treats business as a game, caring little for profit, which irritates the merchant yet makes Siddhartha successful. He watches ordinary people—the 'childlike people'—with amusement as they suffer over money and desire. Kamala teaches him the art of love, and they…
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The turn is the voice he can barely hear (With the Childlike People, paragraph 39): it marks the start of his worry that real life is passing him by. Effect: the next chapter shows that unease growing.

items.text: How does “With the Childlike People” build on “Kamala”? Name one link of cause and effect.
items.lookFor: A causal or structural link between this and the previous chapter.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Cause and effect: Kamala sent him to Kamaswami at the end of “Kamala” (paragraph 65 there), and here the same three skills (paragraph 16) win him his place.

items.text: What can we infer about a character's motives from what they say and do here, as opposed to what they claim?
items.lookFor: An inference about motive supported by a quoted line.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Siddhartha claims trade is only a game, but he keeps doing it for the money it brings Kamala (“The business was good enough to provide him with the money for Kamala” (With the Childlike People, paragraph 37)); Kamaswami claims to value the business, but he values Siddhartha’s calm too (paragraph 31).

items.text: The bell-ringer asked: “Siddhartha calls others 'childlike.' Is he being wise or arrogant?” Now that we have read closely, how would you revise your first answer, and which line changed your mind?
items.lookFor: A revised answer anchored in the text.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: A revised answer should weigh both: he sees real weakness in others (With the Childlike People, paragraph 42, Kamaswami “has no refuge in himself”), but the chapter shows him envying them (paragraph 39), so arrogance is part of it.

items.text: Where does theme appear, and how does it connect this chapter to the larger concern with the search for self-knowledge?
items.lookFor: Look for statements or moments that connect to the book's big ideas.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The theme of the self appears in his talk with Kamala about the refuge inside a person (“Kamaswami is just as smart as I, and still has no refuge in himself.” (With the Childlike People, paragraph 42)); the chapter tests whether that inner refuge survives the city.

items.text: Background: Hesse contrasts spiritual detachment with worldly attachment, echoing Buddhist teaching on desire. How does knowing this change the way you read one moment in the chapter?
items.lookFor: A specific moment reread in light of the context.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Knowing the Buddhist contrast between detachment and attachment shows that his detachment is not the peaceful kind: he is detached from people, not from desire, as paragraph 37 shows.

items.text: A critic might argue: “Siddhartha's superiority is ironic: he is beginning to become what he looks down on.” How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the chapter.
items.lookFor: A defended position with evidence and one counterpoint.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Agree: he despises the childlike people (With the Childlike People, paragraph 37) yet wishes to share their passion (paragraph 39). Counterpoint from the text: he still has the inner refuge Kamaswami lacks (paragraph 42), so he is not yet one of them.

items.text: Which character in this chapter acts most wisely, and which least? Judge them by a standard you name.
items.lookFor: An evaluation using an explicit criterion and evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: With honesty as the standard, Kamala is wisest: she tells him plainly that he loves nobody (paragraph 46); Kamaswami least when he scolds a profitable trip (paragraph 34). Others may judge Siddhartha’s calm the wisest.

items.text: Rewrite one moment of “With the Childlike People” from the point of view of a different character. What does the new angle reveal or hide about detachment among the childlike people?
items.lookFor: A rewrite that keeps the chapter’s events accurate, speaks in the chosen character’s voice, and ends with a sentence on what the new angle shows or hides.
followUps: Which line from the chapter does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Kamaswami’s view of the rice trip (With the Childlike People, paragraphs 33–35) works well: it shows his frustration and hides the inner emptiness Siddhartha later admits.

items.text: Write three questions of your own about “With the Childlike People”: one recall, one “why/how”, and one “should/what if”. Trade with a partner and answer theirs.
items.lookFor: Three questions at three levels, each answerable from the chapter, traded and answered with a line.
followUps: Which of your three questions was hardest to answer from the text, and why?
Which line did your partner use, and does it really answer your why/how question?
items.answerGuidance: Example set: recall, ‘What does Siddhartha write for Kamaswami?’ (paragraph 26); why/how, ‘Why doesn’t Siddhartha worry about losses?’ (paragraph 35); what if, ‘Should Siddhartha have stayed a Samana?’

items.text: Connect this chapter to experience versus teaching: is the link strong or weak so far? What would Hesse need to show next to strengthen it?
items.lookFor: A judgment of thematic development across the work.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Strong: he now learns by experience (trade and love) instead of teaching, yet paragraph 39 shows experience without care is also empty. Hesse needs to show experience that changes him.

items.text: Is the characterization in this chapter effective, or does it feel heavy-handed? Evaluate it as a reader would in a review.
items.lookFor: An evaluative judgment with criteria and evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Effective: Kamaswami and Kamala are shown through dialogue and habits (paragraphs 22–34, 40–47). The narrator’s summaries of the childlike people (paragraph 37) can feel heavy.

items.text: Compare how “With the Childlike People” treats detachment among the childlike people with how another text, film or event you know treats a similar idea. What does Siddhartha see that the other misses?
items.lookFor: A cross-text synthesis.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A comparison should name a story of someone who succeeds without caring and quote “Indeed his soul was not with the trade.” (With the Childlike People, paragraph 37) Siddhartha’s case is that detachment wins money and loses life.

items.text: Predict what “Sansara” will bring, using two clues from this chapter. After reading, evaluate your prediction.
items.lookFor: A prediction or judgment justified with textual clues.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Clues: the dying voice (With the Childlike People, paragraph 39) and his words about not loving (paragraph 47). Prediction: he will sink further into the city’s life and lose touch with the inner voice.

items.text: Design a one-paragraph modern adaptation of this chapter (setting, characters, conflict). What must stay the same for it to still be about detachment among the childlike people?
items.lookFor: A modern setting, characters and conflict that keep the chapter’s core idea, with the one element that must not change named.
followUps: Which line from the chapter does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: A modern version keeps a gifted outsider who succeeds in business and romance while feeling nothing. What must stay is the confession in paragraph 47 that he cannot love.

items.text: What question would you most like to ask Hermann Hesse about this chapter, and what answer do you think the text itself gives?
items.lookFor: A student-generated question answered from evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Example: ‘Does Siddhartha love Kamala?’ The text answers through his own words: no, he practises love as a craft (With the Childlike People, paragraph 47).

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Kamala is a courtesan in an ancient Indian city; the novel treats love as an art she teaches, built on mutual pleasure: “pleasure cannot be taken without giving pleasure” (Hesse, 1922/2015, With the Childlike People, para. 29). Hesse shows that skill without love leaves Siddhartha empty: “Perhaps people of our kind can’t love. The childlike people can; that’s their secret.” (Hesse, 1922/2015, With the Childlike People, para. 47) The narrator calls ordinary people “childlike people”; question that condescension.
contentNotes.studentPreview: The chapter continues the relationship and calls ordinary people 'childlike'.
contentNotes.figurative: Not a self-injury event: “I’ve neither harmed myself nor others by annoyance and hastiness” (With the Childlike People) is about impatience, not about hurting oneself. The framing announcement is given before “Sansara” (lesson 8).
figurativeLines: I’ve neither harmed myself nor others by annoyance and hastiness

Explain success held at arm’s length and the falling-leaf/star contrast, using “Perhaps people of our kind can’t love. The childlike people can; that’s their secret.” (Hesse, 1922/2015, With the Childlike People, para. 47), and compare one critical voice from this unit.

Apply a formal reading to success held at arm’s length and the falling-leaf/star contrast: show how imagery and repetition in “Perhaps people of our kind can’t love. The childlike people can; that’s their secret.” (Hesse, 1922/2015, With the Childlike People, para. 47) build its meaning.

Argue how success held at arm’s length and the falling-leaf/star contrast advances the novel’s claim about teaching versus experience, testing “Perhaps people of our kind can’t love. The childlike people can; that’s their secret.” (Hesse, 1922/2015, With the Childlike People, para. 47) against one later chapter.

Situate success held at arm’s length and the falling-leaf/star contrast within scholarship on Hesse and European representations of Indian thought, stating method and contribution, with “Perhaps people of our kind can’t love. The childlike people can; that’s their secret.” (Hesse, 1922/2015, With the Childlike People, para. 47) as anchor.
